The Chicago Cubs are in the middle of a National League Wild Card Series against the San Diego Padres at Petco Park.
The Padres won the first game of the series 8-0 on Tuesday. Game 2 is scheduled to begin at 9:00 p.m. CDT on Wednesday.
If the Padres win tonight, the Cubs will be eliminated from the playoffs. If the Cubs win, there will be a Game 3 tomorrow. The winner of the series will play the Milwaukee Brewers in the National League Division Series.
Before Wednesday night’s game, Cubs shortstop Dansby Swanson made an honest statement.
Chicago Cubs SS Dansby Swanson Drops Honest Quote Amid Wild Card Series vs. Padres
Via the Chicago Tribune’s Meghan Montemurro on X: Dansby Swanson pregame : “At this time of year, it can be challenging because you go so in depth with the other team & trying to navigate what they’re going to do … I think the greatest reminder is if we do what we do best then we feel like we’re a really good baseball team.”
This season, Swanson posted 3.1 bWAR and a .694 OPS with 19 home runs and 69 RBI over 126 games.

Con batazos de cuatro esquinas de Fernando Tatis Jr., Manny Machado y Xander Bogaerts, sumados a una joya monticular de Michael King, San Diego se impuso 8-0 a Chicago para ponerse a un triunfo de la Serie Divisional.
Los dominicanos Fernando Tatis Jr. y Manny Machado fueron protagonistas en la victoria de San Diego. Foto: MLB.
30 de septiembre de 2026 Hora: 15:43
Padres de San Diego defendió con autoridad su feudo en el primer encuentro de la Serie del Comodín de la Liga Nacional, tras imponerse con una contundente blanqueada de 8-0 sobre Cachorros de Chicago en el Petco Park. La novena californiana cimentó su victoria gracias a una electrizante exhibición ofensiva liderada por Fernando Tatis Jr. y una sobresaliente apertura del derecho Michael King.
El ataque de los frailes no se hizo esperar y castigó temprano al abridor de Chicago, Matthew Boyd. En la conclusión del primer episodio, el poder dominicano se hizo sentir en todo el estadio: Tatis Jr. inauguró la pizarra al depositar la esférica en las gradas del jardín central, seguido por otro cuadrangular de Manny Machado entre los prados izquierdo y derecho. La ofensiva continuó en el tercer capítulo, cuando el antesalista conectó un doblete contra la barda que bañó al jardinero Pete Crow-Armstrong para remolcar a su compatriota y ampliar la ventaja a 3-0.
El arubeño Xander Bogaerts se unió al festín ofensivo contra el zurdo de Cachorros, despachando un dantesco cuadrangular solitario que aterrizó en las gradas del jardín izquierdo. El asedio de San Diego se profundizó en la quinta entrada, cuando Jackson Merrill conectó un sencillo remolcador de dos anotaciones que puso el marcador 6-0. En ese mismo episodio, Ty France pisó la registradora para sumar la séptima rayita del encuentro, aprovechando un pasbol del receptor Carson Kelly.
Más allá de la demostración de poder, Fernando Tatis Jr. demostró otra de las herramientas de su repertorio: la velocidad en las almohadillas. El jardinero causó estragos en la defensiva visitante al estafarse la intermedia y, apoyado en un errático tiro de Kelly hacia la segunda base, completó una fantástica y agresiva carrera hasta el plato para sellar el 8 – 0 definitivo.
Desde el montículo, Michael King maniató por completo a los maderos rivales. El diestro se adjudicó la victoria tras lanzar siete entradas en blanco, en las que apenas toleró un indiscutible, otorgó tres pasaportes y retiró a ocho bateadores por la vía del ponche.
LEA TAMBIÉN:
La serie al mejor de tres compromisos continuará esta noche a las 10:00 p.m., cuando ambas novenas vuelvan a saltar al diamante. Para este duelo crucial, Cachorros de Chicago dependerá de los envíos del derecho Kevin Gausman, quien subirá a la lomita con la obligación de evitar la eliminación. Por su parte, Padres de San Diego le entregarán la esférica a Nick Pivetta, quien tendrá la misión de definir la serie y sellar el pase a la Serie Divisional.

item.content:encoded:
Pete Crow-Armstrong's historic season just produced another staggering number, this time away from the baseball field.
The Chicago Cubs star's one-of-one 2024 Topps Chrome Update MLB Debut Patch Autograph sold for $1.098 million at Goldin.
The PSA Gem Mint 10 card, which also received a PSA 10 autograph grade, features the MLB Debut patch from Crow-Armstrong's first major-league game on September 11, 2023.
It is a massive sale by itself.
The timing makes it even more striking.
Crow-Armstrong just completed a historic 40-home run, 40-stolen base season and helped Chicago reach the postseason. Now, only days later, his signature rookie card has approached the MLB Debut Patch record while Crow-Armstrong and the Cubs enter an elimination game against the San Diego Padres.
$1,098,000: Winning bid for Pete Crow-Armstrong’s debut patch jersey tonight at @GoldinCo.
PCA’s 2024 rookie salary: $740,000. pic.twitter.com/d21WopsNpx
— Darren Rovell (@darrenrovell) September 30, 2026
Pete Crow-Armstrong Card Sells for $1.098 Million
Crow-Armstrong's card was one of the most significant MLB Debut Patch cards to reach the market since Paul Skenes' one-of-one sold in 2025.
Goldin listed the card as Crow-Armstrong's 2024 Topps Chrome Update MLB Debut Patch Autograph 1/1, graded PSA Gem Mint 10 with a PSA/DNA Gem Mint 10 autograph grade.
The $1.098 million result also produced a remarkable comparison highlighted by Rovell.
Crow-Armstrong earned roughly $740,000 during the 2024 season, meaning a collector just paid considerably more for his one-of-one rookie card than the Cubs paid Crow-Armstrong to play an entire major-league season.
But the final auction price may be even more notable for what it narrowly failed to accomplish.
Pete Crow-Armstrong Falls $12,000 Short of Paul Skenes Record
Crow-Armstrong came extraordinarily close to taking down the benchmark for MLB Debut Patch cards.
Skenes' one-of-one 2024 Topps Chrome Update MLB Debut Patch Autograph sold for $1.11 million through Fanatics Collect in March 2025. The price included the buyer's premium and established the Skenes card as the highest-selling MLB Debut Patch at the time.
Crow-Armstrong finished at $1.098 million.
The difference?
Just $12,000.
That puts Crow-Armstrong and Skenes in remarkably similar territory despite playing dramatically different positions and arriving in the majors with different levels of prospect hype.
Skenes was the No. 1 overall pick in the 2023 MLB Draft and won National League Rookie of the Year in his first season. His Debut Patch became a national story even before it surfaced, with the Pittsburgh Pirates famously offering the young collector who pulled it a package that included 30 years of season tickets.
Crow-Armstrong's card reached seven figures after a different catalyst: one of the greatest individual seasons ever produced by a Cubs player.
Pete Crow-Armstrong Made Cubs History Before $1.1 Million Sale
The auction could hardly have closed at a better moment for Crow-Armstrong's hobby profile.
On September 24, Crow-Armstrong stole his 40th base of the season, joining the exclusive 40-40 club after already reaching 45 home runs.
He became just the seventh player in MLB history to record at least 40 homers and 40 stolen bases in the same season. He also became the first Cubs player to accomplish the feat.
And he did it on the same night Chicago clinched an NL Wild Card berth with a 2-1 victory over the Miami Marlins.
Crow-Armstrong entered the postseason hitting .280 with 45 home runs and 107 RBIs while appearing in all 159 Cubs games through the clinching victory.
That transformed the timing of the Goldin auction.
Collectors were not merely bidding on the Debut Patch of a promising young Cubs player.
They were bidding on the Debut Patch of a 24-year-old who had just completed the first 40-40 season in franchise history.
Now the attention shifts back to what Crow-Armstrong can do on the field.
Cubs Face Elimination Against Padres After 8-0 Loss
Chicago enters Game 2 of its Wild Card Series against San Diego needing a victory to keep its season alive.
The Padres routed the Cubs 8-0 in Game 1 on September 29.
San Diego starter Michael King took a no-hit bid into the seventh inning and ultimately allowed only one hit over seven scoreless frames while striking out eight. Fernando Tatis Jr., Manny Machado and Xander Bogaerts each homered for the Padres.
The Cubs will send Kevin Gausman to the mound for Game 2 opposite Nick Pivetta
There is at least one reason for optimism surrounding Crow-Armstrong specifically.
Chicago dominated San Diego during the regular season, winning five of six games and outscoring the Padres 55-28.
Crow-Armstrong was one of the Cubs' biggest problems for San Diego.
He hit .364 with four home runs in the six regular-season meetings.
Chicago will need another performance like that now.
Crow-Armstrong has already produced one of the defining baseball-card sales of 2026 and one of the most statistically significant seasons in Cubs history.
Whether his week is remembered primarily for a $1.098 million card sale or for what happens in October now depends on what Crow-Armstrong and the Cubs do next.

item.content:encoded:
Game 1 of the AL Wild Card Series couldn't have gone much better for the Yankees. On the mound, Cam Schlittler was excellent, blanking the Red Sox for 6.1 impressive innings. Then, led by Ben Rice, the Yankees' offense plated nine runs, pulling away from Boston to go up 1-0 in the series.
Yesterday wasn't just the opening of the Yankees-Red Sox series, though. All three of the Wild Card matchups also got underway on Tuesday, so let's check in on what happened.
AL Wild Card Series Game 1
Chicago White Sox 6, Houston Astros 3
(Chicago leads 1-0)
After jumping out to a 3-0 lead early, the White Sox withstood the Astros and tacked on some more runs late to take the opener of the other AL matchup in Houston.
Facing an Astros' bullpen game, the White Sox got going quickly. With a runner on third in the first, Munetaka Murakami hit a fly ball that was deep enough for Chicago's Sam Antonacci to tag up and score. The next inning, Antonacci did it at the plate, hitting a bases loaded single to bring home two more runs. A Colson Montgomery homer in the fourth and a Chase Meidroth RBI single in the fifth had Chicago up big before Houston showed any resistance.
A two-run shot from Nelson Velázquez in the bottom of the fifth got the Astros on the board, but Chicago got one of those runs back a little while later. Houston countered with one in the eighth and brought the tying run to the plate, but couldn't cash in as the ChiSox held on from there. Amusingly, the Astros have now lost eight consecutive playoff games in Houston since early on in the 2023 playoffs. If Chicago can win one more at Daikin Park either today or tomorrow, they'll not only eliminate Houston but also secure their first playoff series victory since winning the 2005 World Series, over two decades ago. The Astros will have their best pitcher going for them in Hunter Brown, so we'll see if that's enough to keep their season alive.
NL Wild Card Series Game 1
Atlanta Braves 5, Philadelphia Phillies 3
(Atlanta leads 1-0)
Austin Riley's go-ahead eighth inning home run stunned the Phillies to give the Braves the series opener.
The Phillies opened the scoring early when Alec Bohm doubled home a run in the top of the first. Atlanta then answered back with Mike Yastrzemski RBI single. The game remained tied for a while after that as both Chris Sale and Jesús Luzardo put in solid outings; Luzardo hadn't necessarily been expected to even last five innings, as he was still relatively fresh off the IL and threw an inning of relief just to help the Phillies clinch a playof spot on Sunday. Things changed as both teams got to the bullpen, and there were some dramatic swings.
Atlanta took the lead for the first time in the sixth when Ozzie Albies hit an RBI triple thanks to some less-than-stellar fielding from Phillies' center fielder Derek Hill. However, a Ronald Acuña Jr. misplay in the seventh allowed J.T. Realmuto to hit a triple of his own, scoring two runs to put Philly back in front.
Phillies' manager Don Mattingly went for the kill shot by bringing on closer Jhoan Duran in the seventh. He got through that inning fine and came back out for the eighth, facing the heart of Atlanta's order. He got two quick outs before Michael Harris II kept the inning alive with a softly-struck infield single. Duran hit Albies with a pitch after that, bringing Riley to the plate. Duran then left a fastball right in the middle of the zone, and Riley took full advantage, giving Atlanta a lead that Raisel Iglesias held on to in the ninth.
If the Braves win today, then they'll advance to play the two-time defending champion Dodgers in the NLDS. If the Phillies can hold them off behind ace Cristopher Sánchez however, then Game 3 awaits on Thursday.
San Diego Padres 8, Chicago Cubs 0
(San Diego leads 1-0)
Michael King took a no-hitter into the seventh inning as the Padres' offense crushed Cubs pitching in the late night game out west.
The Cubs' story this season is that they have an excellent offense and poor pitching, ranking first and last in fWAR respectively. However in Game 1, only one of those things proved true. Fernando Tatis Jr. and Manny Machado both hit first inning home runs against Matthew Boyd, getting San Diego off to the perfect start, from which they only added on to their lead.
Meanwhile, the Cubs offense couldn't do much against King. The former Yankee didn't allow a hit until Nico Hoerner singled with one out in the seventh. In total, King shut out Chicago over seven frames, allowing just the one hit and three walks, striking out eight.
In the ninth inning, Padres' pitcher Joe Musgrove returned to the majors after a two-year absence while recovering from Tommy John surgery. He allowed a couple Cubs to reach base, but did end up throwing a scoreless inning.

Fernando Tatis Jr. Talks Padres' Dominant MLB Playoffs G1 Win vs. Cubs, 'Beautiful Baseball Night'
Fernando Tatís Jr. reflected on what was essentially a perfect night for the San Diego Padres on Tuesday, as they cruised to an 8-0 win over the Chicago Cubs in Game 1 of their National League Wild Card Series.
Speaking to reporters following the one-sided victory, Tatís said, "We couldn't have scripted it any better than what happened tonight. Today was a beautiful baseball night for every San Diegan."
Playing in front of over 47,000 fans at Petco Park in San Diego, the Padres poured it on from the get-go, as they led 2-0 after one inning and 7-0 through five.
Tatís was a big part of the Padres' offensive success in Game 1, as he launched a solo home run to lead off the bottom of the first inning.
All told, Tatís went 2-for-3, walked once, stole a base and scored three runs to go along with the one homer and one RBI.
Veteran third baseman Manny Machado also homered and drove in a pair, while starting pitcher Michael King authored a masterpiece, allowing one hit and no runs, while walking three and striking out eight over seven innings.
King and the San Diego pitching staff notably shut down Cubs outfielder and NL MVP front-runner Pete Crow-Armstrong, as he went 0-for-3 with three strikeouts and one walk.
The Padres are now just one win away from advancing to the National League Division Series for the second time in the past three seasons.
They will send Nick Pivetta to the mound for Wednesday night's Game 2 of the NLWCS, while Chicago will counter with Kevin Gausman.

Manny Machado Calls Out Reporter's Blue Jacket in Video Before Padres' MLB Playoffs Series vs. Cubs
Before Tuesday's NL Wild Card Game 1 against the Chicago Cubs, San Diego Padres veteran slugger Manny Machado isn't interested in disloyalty.
So when Machado noticed CBS 8's Karthik Venkataraman wearing Cubs colors, he couldn't help but question why the San Diego-based reporter appeared to be aligning with the enemy.
"Hey, aren't you from San Diego? Why are you wearing blue?" Machado said, interrupting Venkataraman's question.
"Yeah, you like it? You don't like it?" Venkataraman asked him.
"Obviously not," Machado replied.
The Padres lost the regular-season series against the Cubs 5-1, so Machado and company will need all the support they can get in their upcoming playoff series.

29 Sep 2026, 06:49 GMT+10

(Photo credit: David Frerker)
The Chicago Cubs eliminated the San Diego Padres from the postseason a year ago and then scored 55 runs while going 5-1 against them this season.
But nobody is expecting that type of one-sided matchup to continue as the Padres are hotter than lava entering Tuesday night's National League wild-card series opener against visiting Chicago.
The Padres (91-71) are a sizzling 41-18 since July 24, transforming a bumbling campaign into a third straight postseason berth, a first in franchise history.
In the final days of the season, San Diego overtook the Cubs (89-73) to secure the No. 4 seed, granting the Padres home-field advantage in the best-of-three series. Chicago, the No. 5 seed, hosted at Wrigley Field last season and beat the Padres in three games in the wild-card round.
Playing the series at pitcher-friendly Petco Park could lessen the Cubs' offensive advantage. Chicago led the majors with 850 runs this season, while the Padres scored 722.
The Cubs feature leading NL MVP candidate Pete Crow-Armstrong, who recorded a 40-40 season by tying for the major league lead with 45 homers and adding 41 steals. He also led the majors with 84 extra-base hits and 119 runs.
Crow-Armstrong batted .364 (8-for-22) with four homers and 10 RBIs against San Diego this season.
'I'm looking forward to playing a really good ballclub and getting another crack at them and starting this playoffs off on a high note,' Crow-Armstrong said Monday.
San Diego's Manny Machado batted a career-low .217 but smacked 30 homers, marking the eighth time in his career he has hit at least that many.
More important to the Padres is Fernando Tatis Jr., who didn't hit his first homer until May 30 and had just five at the All-Star break. He hit 20 blasts after the break and was a major catalyst for the team's torrid 59-game finish.
'It's a baseball game. We have to get 27 outs and hopefully be the last team standing,' Machado said.
Right-hander Michael King (12-10, 3.21 ERA) will start for the Padres against Cubs left-hander Matthew Boyd (10-5, 3.91).
King has made two career postseason starts, both in 2024 for the Padres. The most memorable one came in Game 1 of the wild-card series against the Atlanta Braves when he tossed seven shutout innings and struck out 12.
King gave up one hit and struck out three in one inning of relief against the Cubs in the 2025 postseason series, his lone appearance against them with the Padres. He also twice faced Chicago in relief when he was with the New York Yankees.
'Very professional lineup,' King said of the Cubs. 'They were first in runs this year and it shows. I keep saying that when the pitcher executes, we have the upper hand so I have to make sure I am executing throughout and putting up as many zeroes as I can.'
Chicago's Alex Bregman is 7-for-8 with two doubles against King.
Bregman surged over the final two months, delivering 17 homers and 46 RBIs to get his season outputs to 28 and 93, respectively.
Bregman is playing with multiple fractures in his left cheek after getting hit by a foul ball off the bat of teammate Michael Busch during a game on Sept. 20.
Boyd, 35, is 0-1 with a 1.66 ERA in seven playoff appearances (six starts). He was 0-1 with a 2.79 ERA in three starts for Chicago last postseason and gave up one run and four hits over 4 1/3 innings when the Cubs beat the Padres in Game 1 of last year's wild-card series.
'The Padres are one of the hottest teams in baseball the past few weeks,' Boyd said. 'That's not surprising. We've seen them firsthand -- this year, last year. I always firmly believe that it's more about what's in this clubhouse and less about what's on the other side. Take care of your business.'
Boyd is 2-1 with a 4.43 ERA in four regular-season outings against San Diego. Machado is 9-for-20 (.450) with a homer and four doubles against Boyd.
The winner of this series faces the Milwaukee Brewers in the National League Division Series.
--Field Level Media

Back in July, we celebrated the All-Star Game by looking at which participants had the best chance of eventually earning induction into the Hall of Fame. The likes of Bryce Harper, Justin Verlander, and Mike Trout all were locks, and rightfully so.
But as the MLB playoffs prepare to kick off, Verlander and Trout are once again sitting at home. Harper and the Phillies survived a near-collapse to secure a Wild Card seed, and he’s one of many postseason participants who could — and in his case, should — find themselves in the Hall of Fame one day.
Besides the obvious counting stats, what makes a Hall of Famer? As we’ve previously noted, baseball fans have recently accepted 40 bWAR as the standard for a remarkable career. Immaculate Grid is to thank on that front, even if there are players who have cleared that mark but don’t feel like Hall of Famers. Astros shortstop Carlos Correa, who is injured but has a 47.1 bWAR, is a perfect example, and he didn’t crack our list.
Instead, let’s turn our attention to someone who may very well become the second unanimous electee when his time comes.
Honorable mention: The Shohei Ohtani tier
Barring any unprecedented rule changes, Hall of Fame candidates must have 10 full seasons worth of experience for eligibility. That means Shohei Ohtani would technically be ineligible if he retired tomorrow, so he won’t land in the “lock” tier.
But Ohtani has always been a unicorn, so him having his own category makes all too much sense. We can all agree that, at this time next year, Ohtani should be a lock on that list.
Not yet eligible, but…
These guys don’t get their own table, but we wanted to address their situations ahead of the playoffs.
- Aroldis Chapman, P, Boston Red Sox: Off the numbers alone, Chapman and his 402 saves (ninth all-time) likely warrant induction. However, he also served a 30-game suspension in 2016 for violating the league’s domestic violence policy. It’s difficult to envision him earning the 75 percent required for election. Recent voting trends don’t work in favor of those who have been suspended for performance-enhancing drugs (more on that soon) or off-field incidents.
- Cam Schlittler, SP, New York Yankees and Jacob Misirowski, SP, Milwaukee Brewers: We’re lumping these two together because both will be trending during the playoffs. Just because these two are likely to win their league’s respective Cy Young Awards doesn’t mean they’re guaranteed a spot in Cooperstown. Heck, we don’t even know if they’ll pitch long enough to appear on a ballot! But, you know how baseball fans are.
- Fernando Tatis Jr., 2B/RF, San Diego Padres: As things currently stand, Tatis has no chance of getting into the Hall of Fame. Voters have made it clear that those who serve PED-related suspensions, as Tatis did in 2022, aren’t welcome in Cooperstown unless they buy a ticket. That said, we’re including him here
- Tarik Skubal, SP, Los Angeles Dodgers: Skubal became the 23rd pitcher in MLB history to win multiple Cy Young Awards, which will appeal to voters who prefer the "dominant" peak. But we’d like to see at least two or three more years of him being at least above-average. He’s also only seven seasons in, so he has a lot of work left.
On pace to make it into Cooperstown
- Alex Bregman, Chicago Cubs - 48.9 bWAR
- Matt Olson, Atlanta Braves - 44.2 bWAR
- Yordan Alvarez, DH, Houston Astros - 30.5 bWAR
These three have team success, specifically at least one World Series ring, working in their favor. Alvarez is likely to win AL MVP, and the 29-year-old is young enough that clearing 40 bWAR shouldn’t be an issue so long as healthy.
Bregman turns 33 next March, and his bWAR is likely far greater than you’d have guessed. But is he truly on a Hall of Fame trajectory? He's nowhere close to 2,000 hits (1,411) or 300 home runs (237), both of which are vital numbers when playing the hot corner.
Consider, though, that Bregman has averaged 24 home runs, 84 RBIs, 32 doubles, and 4.6 bWAR over the last five years. He’s under contract through 2030, and exceeded all of those numbers (28 home runs, 93 RBIs, 33 doubles, and 5.8 bWAR) this season.
If Bregman were to continue averaging those numbers, he’d end the 2031 season with 333 home runs, roughly 2,200 hits, and 481 doubles. Oh, and his bWAR would be right around 72.0, so we imagine he’d be a first-ballot inductee.
Unfortunately for him and Olson, the possibility of a work stoppage could have a monumental impact on their final counting stats. Which leads us into…
Borderline veterans
- Giancarlo Stanton, New York Yankees - 47.0 bWAR
- Zack Wheeler, Philadelphia Phillies - 46.6 bWAR
- Gerrit Cole, SP, New York Yankees - 45.8 bWAR
- Christian Yelich, Milwaukee Brewers - 45.1 bWAR
- Xander Bogaerts, SS, San Diego Padres - 44.3 bWAR
- Max Fried, P, New York Yankees - 32.3 bWAR
- Kyle Schwarber, OF/DH, Philadelphia Phillies - 22.3 bWAR
Stanton and Schwarber’s cases are likely dependent on whether they surpass 500 home runs. The latter will enter next season at 385 homers, and he turns 34 in March. But the looming work stoppage could significantly affect his chances of reaching 400 anytime soon.
As for Stanton, multiple lower-body injuries limited him to three homers in 24 games. Although he has 466 career home runs, the 2017 NL MVP turns 37 in November and is a free agent after next year.
The only members of the 500-home run club who aren’t in the Hall of Fame are either ineligible or have ties to performance-enhancing drugs. It’d be pretty remarkable if Schwarber and Stanton both cleared the historic total yet fell short of Cooperstown.
Personally, Wheeler and Cole are probably the only ones who will have a legitimate Hall of Fame résumé when they become eligible. The rest of those guys are Hall of Very Good at best. Much like Skubal, we need two or three more elite seasons from Fried before we’d even consider voting for him.
Go ahead and make the Hall of Fame plaque
- Mookie Betts, Los Angeles Dodgers - 79.0 bWAR
- Freddie Freeman, Los Angeles Dodgers - 66.8 bWAR
- Paul Goldschmidt, New York Yankees - 65.1 bWAR
- Aaron Judge, New York Yankees - 64.2 bWAR
- Manny Machado, San Diego Padres - 63.3 bWAR
- Chris Sale, Atlanta Braves - 62.7 bWAR
- José Ramírez, Cleveland Guardians - 60.3 bWAR
- Bryce Harper, Philadelphia Phillies - 56.9 bWAR
- Jose Altuve, Houston Astros - 53.4 bWAR
Outside of Goldschmidt and Sale, none of these names are overly surprising. And no, the Astros’ sign-stealing scandal shouldn’t impact Altuve, especially not after Carlos Beltrán just entered the Hall of Fame.
Goldschmidt currently ranks 143rd on the all-time bWAR list, and only 31 men above him aren’t already enshrined. But of the 20 who are or were eligible, most came up short for PED or off-field reasons. The question then becomes whether he’s wearing a Diamondbacks or Cardinals cap, or if he opts for the blank hat.
Although Sale turns 38 next March, he has a lifetime 2.95 ERA and 2,779 strikeouts, putting him within range of reaching 3,000. There’s absolutely no reason why he shouldn’t be a first-ballot selection.
As for the rest? You know a Hall of Famer when you see one, and they more than meet the expectations.

SAN DIEGO (AP) — Manny Machado hit a three-run homer and the San Diego Padres beat the Arizona Diamondbacks 10-7 on Saturday to secure the No. 4 seed in the National League playoffs.
San Diego will host every game in a best-of-three Wild Card Series against the fifth-seeded Chicago Cubs beginning Tuesday. The winner will face the NL Central champion Milwaukee Brewers in a best-of-five Division Series.
The Cubs eliminated the Padres 2-1 in the wild-card round at Chicago last season.
Xander Bogaerts also went deep for the Padres (90-71), who clinched their club-record third straight 90-win season and seventh in team history. They earned their franchise-best third consecutive postseason berth with a 4-2 win Thursday night at the NL West champion Los Angeles Dodgers.
The Diamondbacks had their six-game winning streak snapped but remain alive for the NL's third wild-card spot. They are one game behind Philadelphia going into Sunday's season finales and hold the tiebreaker. The Phillies lost their fourth straight game, 12-1 to AL East champion Tampa Bay.
Arizona's Gabriel Moreno hit an RBI single and went 1 for 3 with a walk to keep his average at .311, just ahead of injured Phillies infielder Luis Arraez (.310) in the race for the NL batting title.
Moreno's spot in the order came up after Mason Miller loaded the bases with no outs in the ninth, but the Diamondbacks sent pinch-hitter Adrian Del Castillo to the plate and he struck out. Miller allowed three runs.
Machado hit a 1-1 pitch from Jose Cabrera (0-4) into the home run porch in the right-field corner for a 6-4 lead in the fourth. That gave Machado his eighth career 30-homer season, tying Arizona's Nolan Arenado and Philadelphia's Kyle Schwarber for the most among active players.
It was his fourth 30-homer season with San Diego, tying Adrian Gonzalez for the most in team history.
The Diamondbacks went ahead 4-3 in the top of the fourth on James McCann's two-run homer to straightaway center off Walker Buehler.
Arizona led 2-1 in the third before the Padres went in front on Ty France's RBI groundout and Gavin Sheets' RBI double that center fielder Tim Tawa lost in the lights and twilight sky.
Bogaerts hit a solo homer in the two-run fifth, and Jake Cronenworth added a two-run single in the sixth.
Yuki Matsui (5-1) got the win in relief.
Up next
Diamondbacks RHP Michael Soroka (9-5, 3.31 ERA) is scheduled to pitch the season finale Sunday. The Padres hadn't announced a starter.

The San Diego Padres just made the playoffs, and they're looking to move up to clinch the top spot so they can stay at home through the wild-card round. Not many people believed this was possible back in June when the team was playing .500 baseball, but one who did was third baseman Manny Machado, who professed faith in the team's ability to turn things around throughout the season.
It's been a strange season for Machado. He hasn't been good, but he has been steady, and he's contributed power. The average posted on the scoreboard every night is still ugly at .215, but Machado currently has 29 home runs and counting.
Dennis Lin of The Athletic did an intriguing story on Machado, and he noted how some of his teammates have reacted to the third baseman's struggles, which are still punctuated here and there with some great games.
Ty France was one. France has had a breakout campaign, and he noted that a lot of what he does is watching how Machando "goes about his business."
But the spotlight is about to get a lot more focused. The Padres lost last year because their three stars didn't hit, and in some ways Machado's struggles last year against the Chicago Cubs in the wild-card series were a harbinger of what was to come.
Machado went 1-for'10 against the Cubs with a two-run homer — i.e., he hit for power but didn't hit for much else. Fernando Tatis Jr. and Jackson Merrill were also shut down, and the result was a team that couldn't score enough runs to win games.
The Padres have been that at times this season, and if they do that again, they'll be heading on vacation, regardless of where they do it in the postseason.
France noted that Machado's steady, calm approach to his struggles has been a key in San Diego's recent surge, as he said that he's played for teams where the leaders are "full of panic and anxiety and stress" and it spreads throughout the team.
Machado still hunts mistakes as well as any hitter in the game, although he misses a lot more than he used to. His homer against Los Angeles Dodgers starter Yoshinobu Yamamoto on Wednesday left the bat at an exit velocity of 108.6 mph, per Lin, and France said the value Machado brings to the locker room is "irreplaceable."
But the focus on dealing with the Padres lineup will be the same, and whether Machado can step up and do more is a big question going into the playoffs.

When the San Diego Padres were 50-53 going into a series in Miami on July 24, they were perhaps one more series loss away from being sellers at the MLB trade deadline.
Since then, they’ve posted the major leagues’ top record at 39-17, clinching their third straight playoff berth and their fifth in seven years with a 4-2 win Thursday night at the Los Angeles Dodgers.
Now San Diego has a chance to stay at home for the wild-card round of the National League playoffs — if it can take care of business in its final series of the season, starting Friday night against the Arizona Diamondbacks.
The Padres (89-70) are one game ahead of the Chicago Cubs for the first wild-card berth and two games ahead of the Philadelphia Phillies. They have won six straight series, mostly against sub-.500 teams, though they bookended it by taking two of three from the New York Yankees and the Dodgers.
“I think we learned a lot from those struggles,” Padres third baseman Manny Machado said. “Baseball’s a hard game, man, but we learned a lot from the struggles. To come in here and take a series from this team means a lot. We haven’t done that much lately.”
It marked the first time since April 2024 that San Diego has won a series at Dodger Stadium.
In the midst of a full-fledged celebration, center fielder Jackson Merrill sounded a cautionary note.
“We’ve still got three important games left,” he said.
The first of those will be pitched by Casey Mize (6-9, 3.96 ERA), who might be pitching for his spot on the wild-card roster. Mize was roughed up for five hits and five runs with five walks in three innings Saturday night during his team’s 7-6, 10-inning win over Miami.
Formerly with Detroit, Mize coughed up eight runs in 3 1/3 innings in his first start for the Padres in a 10-4 loss on Aug. 5 at Arizona.
As for the Diamondbacks (85-74), they flew into San Diego on Thursday evening after a 12-8 win in Colorado secured a series sweep that kept them in the wild-card hunt. They trail Philadelphia by two games and the Cubs by three.
“We came on this road trip knowing exactly what we needed to do and that’s win each day,” Arizona catcher James McCann said. “The focus and the talk in this clubhouse has been go 1-0 every day. That’s what we’ve done so far and that’s what we’re going to look to continue to do.
“We can’t control what other teams are doing, but we can control the way that we approach each and every day.”
Arizona has won its last five games to keep its hopes alive and will have one of its best pitchers, Brandon Pfaadt (7-3, 3.72), starting the series opener. The right-hander last worked on Saturday night in his team’s 5-3 home win over the Yankees, allowing four hits and one run over 4 1/3 innings with a walk and three strikeouts.
Pfaadt is 2-0 in three outings this year against the Padres. He has won both of his starts, yielding one unearned run in 12 2/3 innings, and is 5-3 with a 3.82 ERA in 12 career appearances against them.
In his career, Pfaadt is 5-3 with an ERA of 3.82 and 12 starts in his career against San Diego. He has made one career start against
The teams have split their first 10 meetings this year, including a four-game series in San Diego from July 6-9.

item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — If there are any messages being sent this week, they’re subtle ones.
The Dodgers and Padres have become quite the rivalry in recent years. The Padres’ stars, particularly Fernando Tatis Jr. and Manny Machado, get on the nerves of Dodger fans. San Diegans, with their tendency to dislike all things associated with the metropolis to the north – except for that segment of folks who still can’t totally let go of the Chargers – relish the opportunity to, well, beat L.A.
Consider: When the Padres finally slew the dragon from the north as the late Peter Seidler, then owner, memorably predicted, they did everything but push back closing time in the Gaslamp Quarter. The roar that accompanied that 2022 National League Division Series victory might still be echoing in Petco Park all these years later, so hungry were Padres fans to take down the Dodgers, especially after L.A. had beaten them on neutral ground in the 2020 COVID-19-influenced postseason.
It’s also fairly obvious that the Dodgers’ 2022 failure, followed by a 2023 NLDS sweep by the Arizona Diamondbacks, helped create the monster in Chavez Ravine that is currently terrorizing all of baseball, including the segment of ownership that is willing to push the game to the brink in its zeal for a salary cap that labor has no intention of ever accepting.
You think Andrew Friedman and the rest of the Dodgers’ front office didn’t redouble their efforts following those two playoff flameouts? The mere possibility of a three-peat now should be proof of how much those losses stung. And the hype video in Dodger Stadium these nights is a pretty accurate representation of the state of mind here, the feeling that the Dodgers and their fans not only don’t care that they’ve become baseball’s villains, they relish it.
As the voiceover narrator puts it, “What’s wrong with being the bad guy? If being the best makes you bad, so be it. … If we’re being honest, sometimes it’s fun to root for the bad guy. … You need teams like us so you can point your finger and say, ‘That’s the bad guy.’”
The villainy works both ways, of course. Witness the first inning of the first game of this current series on Tuesday night.
Machado provokes strong reactions in L.A. because (a) he spent the final months of the 2018 season with the Dodgers, (b) his style of play was, shall we say, overly energy efficient – or, as he put it, “I’m not the type of player that’s going to be ‘Johnny Hustle’” – and (c) after that season he signed a 10-year, $300 million free agent contract with San Diego.
So, in Game 1 on Tuesday night, Brock Stewart’s first pitch to Machado knocked him down. The crowd jeered, loudly, and Machado took the moment to sit there and nod his head as if to say, “Yeah, it’s on.”
There were no further dust-ups in the first two games of this series, a 7-0 Dodgers victory on Tuesday night and a 5-1 Padres victory on Wednesday.
This wasn’t quite on the order of the series in June 2025, when then-Padres manager Mike Shildt and Dodgers outfielder Andy Pages exchanged words on the first night after Pages was hit by a pitch, Tatis and Shohei Ohtani were both plunked and Dodgers manager Dave Roberts was eventually ejected the second night, and Roberts and Shildt exchanged words at home plate after Tatis was hit again in Game 3.
Actually, the teams have been comparatively sedate in 2026. As for their fans on social media … ah, we’ll leave that alone.
But a Dodgers-Padres postseason series would almost certainly bring all of the emotions to the surface. Remember, the Padres not only knocked the Dodgers off in 2022 but had them on the ropes in 2024, one game away from another early elimination, before an 8-0 victory in a Game 4 bullpen game in San Diego reversed the momentum.
Also, keep in mind that after the Padres had knocked out Clayton Kershaw in an early season game in San Diego in 2023, a “Crying Kershaw” meme was posted on the Petco Park scoreboard. Consider, too, that the Dodgers gave fans replica Kershaw World Series rings before the first game of this series.
Coincidence? I think not.
And so here we are again. Los Angeles and San Diego split the first two games of their series this week, and while it might not be a major topic of conversation in either clubhouse this week you can bet these teams are casting wary eyes at each other, aware that fate could throw them together in yet another best-of-five (or maybe even best-of-seven) classic.
First things first. After Wednesday night’s game the Dodgers were still one victory or one Atlanta defeat away from clinching the No. 2 spot among division winners and the right to skip the best-of-three Wild Card round. The Padres’ magic number for clinching a wild card berth, likewise, was one.
Will Smith wasn’t about to look ahead. “We’re still approaching it as trying to win some ballgames,” he said. “I don’t think we’ve clinched the bye yet, so we’re still trying to do that.”
But Roberts acknowledged that it was in the back of his mind.
“Yeah, yeah, it’s in there,” he said.
“We’re pretty familiar with these guys. But yeah, absolutely. You know, we’re gathering information on Robbie Ray (Wednesday night’s starter), and, you know, there are guys in the ’pen and (Michael) King (Monday) and we’ll see (Nick) Pivetta (Thursday). So, certainly.”
And, Roberts noted before Wednesday night’s game in response to a question from San Diego Union-Tribune columnist Tom Krasovic, “They’re a thorn in our side and great competition.”
The feeling, I’m sure, is mutual. And while it might wear both teams out, don’t you wish these teams went back to facing each other 18 times during the regular season instead of 13, as they did this season?
Come to think of it, a five-game playoff series … nah, let’s not get too far ahead of ourselves.

The Houston Astros keep leaving the door open for the Texas Rangers to win the American League West.
The Rangers keep refusing to walk through.
The Rangers will look to avoid a costly sweep on Thursday afternoon when they face the New York Mets in the finale of a three-game interleague series in Arlington, Texas.
Right-hander Kumar Rocker (5-11, 4.47 ERA) will start for the Rangers against Mets left-hander Zac Thornton (5-5, 3.40).
The Mets dealt another blow to the Rangers' playoff hopes Wednesday night, when former Texas second baseman Marcus Semien hit the tie-breaking homer in the eighth inning of New York's 7-2 victory.
Despite the defeat, the Rangers (78-80) remain tied for first place with the Astros atop the AL West thanks to Houston's 6-5, 10-inning loss to the Seattle Mariners later Wednesday night.
The Rangers also are still in the race for the final AL wild-card berth, trailing the Chicago White Sox by three games.
Thus, the most realistic path to the postseason for the Rangers remains winning the AL West. But Houston won the season series over the Rangers 9-4, which means Texas would need to take the division outright.
The Astros are just 8-12 since Sept. 1 -- a span in which the Rangers have gone 10-10. With a chance to establish themselves as the division favorite over the past two games, Texas has been outscored 13-5 by the Mets (73-85), who have been under .500 since April 11.
'We have to play perfectly the rest of the way,' Rangers first baseman Jake Burger said. 'Obviously, we don't want to be in this situation where we're at now. But we have to go out there and try and get four wins.'
The role of spoiler has become familiar for the Mets, who are 26-19 since trading eight veterans before the Aug. 3 trade deadline. New York has won series in that span over the Rangers as well as the AL East champion Tampa Bay Rays along with the Cleveland Guardians, San Diego Padres and Philadelphia Phillies, all of whom are on the verge of locking up playoff spots.
'That's all we can do right now -- we're not in it, so we want to definitely play our best baseball,' said Semien, who played for the Rangers from 2022 through 2025 and helped them win the World Series in 2023. 'I told the guys we look like we're playing free, and I think that's to our advantage right now.'
Rocker didn't factor into the decision in his most recent start last Friday, when he gave up one run over 4 1/3 innings in the Rangers' 7-1 win over the Toronto Blue Jays.
Thornton earned the victory last Friday after allowing two runs over six innings as the Mets beat the Philadelphia Phillies 6-3.
Rocker has never opposed the Mets, who selected him in the first round of the 2021 draft but did not sign him due to concerns about his shoulder and elbow. He underwent shoulder surgery in September 2021 and was drafted by the Rangers in the first round in 2022 before undergoing Tommy John surgery in 2023.
Thornton has never faced the Rangers.

LOS ANGELES (AP) Manny Machado homered and drove in three runs as the San Diego Padres beat the Los Angeles Dodgers 5-1 on Wednesday night to take sole possession of the top spot in the National League wild-card standings.
The loss snapped the NL West champions' 11-game home winning streak and kept the Dodgers (97-61) from clinching at least the No. 2 seed in the National League and a first-round playoff bye. To secure that, they still need one win or an Atlanta loss.
The Padres (88-70) were prevented from clinching their franchise-record third consecutive playoff berth when Arizona beat Colorado 5-3. But they need just one win or a Diamondbacks loss to punch their ticket to the postseason.
San Diego leads Chicago (87-71) and Philadelphia (87-71) by one game for the first National League wild card, a spot that would bring home-field advantage throughout a best-of-three Wild Card Series.
In his return from the injured list, Shohei Ohtani went 1 for 4 with a single, a walk and two strikeouts for Los Angeles. He went down swinging with the bases loaded to end the fourth inning. His long drive to center field was caught near the wall leading off the eighth.
Dodgers starter Yoshinobu Yamamoto (14-9) retired nine of his first 10 batters before the Padres got to him in the fourth and fifth innings of his final regular-season start.
San Diego grabbed a 2-0 lead on Machado's 409-foot homer to center that scored Dustin Harris, who was hit by a pitch from Yamamoto leading off the fourth.
The Dodgers closed to 2-1 in the bottom half when Teoscar Hernández scored on Tommy Edman's sacrifice fly on the first pitch from reliever David Morgan.
The Padres extended their lead to 4-1 in the fifth on Yamamoto's second career throwing error and Machado's shallow sacrifice fly.
Freddy Fermin's RBI single in the ninth scored Samad Taylor, who walked and stole second and third on consecutive pitches by reliever Blake Treinen, making it 5-1.
Bradgley Rodriguez (4-3) got the win with two scoreless innings of relief.

item.content:encoded:
San Diego Padres third baseman Manny Machado is one of the most accomplished players of this generation, but will he be able to add a World Series title to his star-studded resume?
Bryce Harper. Aaron Judge. Jacob deGrom. Tarik Skubal. Besides being certifiable MLB royalty, what do these players have in common? Despite collectively owning a number of Most Valuable Player and Cy Young Awards, and making a total of 20 playoff appearances over 46 combined seasons, none of them has been able to participate in that final champagne shower of the season, emblematic of the World Series champion.
The list also included third baseman Manny Machado of the San Diego Padres, who, according to the writer, "has been one of the best third basemen in the game for more than a decade," but aside from a 2018 deadline-day trade that sent him from the Baltimore Orioles to the Los Angeles Dodgers, who would lose that year's World Series to the Boston Red Sox, Machado has not otherwise appeared on the game's biggest stage, let alone won the ultimate title.
Still, it's safe to say that Machado has presided over the most successful period in the franchise's history. Since Machado signed with the Padres as a free agent before the 2019 season after 6-1/2 years with the Orioles and two months with the Dodgers, San Diego has made the playoffs four times (2020, 2022, 2024 and 2025).
The Padres also stand on the verge of qualifying again this season, which they can do with a win Wednesday night against the Los Angeles Dodgers and a loss by the Arizona Diamondbacks to the Colorado Rockies. Should they earn an NL wild-card spot, it would be the first time San Diego has made the playoffs three seasons in a row. Not bad for a franchise that made the playoffs a grand total of five times in its 50 years of existence before Machado's arrival.
Machado's contribution to this growing history of success comes in the form of being one of the sport's most reliable players. In his 15th season overall and eighth with the Padres, Machado has been a model of consistency. He's been an All-Star seven times, is a three-time Silver Slugger winner, two-time Gold Glove recipient, has finished in the top 10 in MVP voting five times and compiled a 63.4 career WAR.
Even with all those honors, Machado's most significant "ability" may be his "availability." The only time he's missed any significant time with injury was during his second full season in Baltimore when he appeared in 82 games. Since joining San Diego, Machado has appeared in less than 150 games only once, when he played 138 in 2023, and he even appeared in all 60 games during the COVID-shortened 2020 season.
This year, he's played in 153 of San Diego's 157 games as of Wednesday and, after a stuttering start to the season (.182 average and .616 OPS through May 20), Machado has looked more Manny-like in the ensuing four months. As of Wednesday, he has 28 home runs with 84 RBIs, both of which are within career norms, though his average and OPS (.218 and .710, respectively) are career lows and his 139 strikeouts are a career high.
That being said, with 2,193 hits at the age of 33, Machado is the one active player "with the best chance of reaching 3,000 hits," according to a July 2025 report from The Athletic via The Sporting News. A similar report from MLB.com, also from July 2025, noted that with more than 2,000 hits and 350 home runs at the time, Machado was the 12th player in MLB history to reach those milestones in their age-32 season or earlier. The list includes Hall of Famers Hank Aaron, Lou Gehrig, Mickey Mantle, Willie Mays and Frank Robinson, and contemporaries Miguel Cabrera, Albert Pujols and Alex Rodriguez.
With continued good health and a contract that runs through the 2033 season, Machado will have ample opportunity to join the 3,000-hit/500-HR club, an exclusive group that includes just seven members: Aaron, Mays, Cabrera, Pujols, Rodriguez, Eddie Murray and Rafael Palmeiro.
But that's a discussion for another day. Of more immediate concern, do Machado and the Padres have what it takes to qualify for the playoffs and then make that magical run to a World Series championship? If the playoffs started Wednesday night, they'd travel to meet the Atlanta Braves in the three-game wild-card round. A win there would send them to Los Angeles to take on the Dodgers. Winning that series would match them in the NLCS against one of the Milwaukee Brewers, Chicago Cubs or Philadelphia Phillies. The likeliest World Series opponents would be the Tampa Bay Rays or New York Yankees.
This San Diego squad has definitely been built with a deep playoff run in mind. Michael King, Casey Mize, Robbie Ray and Nick Pivetta headline a solid rotation with the red-hot Fernando Tatis Jr. and Jackson Merrill pacing an offense that has helped the Padres win 13 or their past 15 games going into Wednesday night. The real key to postseason success lies in a shutdown bullpen led by Mason Miller, Adrian Morejon and Bradgley Rodriguez, who has been predicted to be a surprise postseason star.
And don't expect Manny Machado, who has been a foundational piece of this franchise for seven seasons, to be solely along for the ride as the Padres chase World Series glory.

item.content:encoded:
Third base wasn't viewed as a strong position entering 2026, and it doesn't look much stronger. Sure, we had players like Sal Stewart, Miguel Vargas, and Kevin McGonigle breaking out and establishing themselves as the next generation of the position, perhaps, and that ain't nothing.
But we also had deeply disappointing seasons from Jose Ramirez, Jazz Chisholm, Manny Machado, Austin Riley, Maikel Garcia, Bo Bichette, Eugenio Suarez, and Noelvi Marte, all of whom were drafted in the top 10 at the position. It would not be an overstatement to say that eight of the top 10 at the position busted, and you can throw Matt Chapman (3B12 in ADP) and Addison Barger (3B14) in there, too, to round it out.
So, yeah, we needed the breakouts. Because a lot of the old standbys let us down and it's not like the breakouts are without their flaws or concerns – any player who has only done it once is going to enter the next season with at least some question marks. Looking ahead to 2027, Junior Caminero might be the only sure thing at the position. He's going to be a first-rounder no matter what, but if you're the type to play position scarcity games, you might need to make sure you reach for him no matter where you're picking. Because if not, you're going to be left with a big question mark at an important position.
The toughest players to rank at third base
Jose Ramirez, Guardians
There are those who will argue Ramirez is very easy to rank. Some will say you should take his decline at face value; when a 34-year-old starts to fall off, they don't generally get it back. Ramirez enters the final week of the season hitting .237, his worst mark since 2015, while his 12 homers are his fewest since 2016. Sure, there was a mid-season hand surgery to blame it on, but to reiterate an earlier point: You probably shouldn't expect a 34-year-old to be healthier than he was in the past. Just take the numbers and the decline at face value.
That's one approach you can take. But I don't think it'll be mine. Because, despite the mediocre production, it doesn't actually look like Ramirez's skill set has declined much at all. His strikeout rate is up, but at 12.9%, it's still within a percentage point of his career mark, while his walk rate is actually his highest since 2021. His .306 wOBA is his worst mark since 2015, but his .329 expected wOBA is basically right in line with what he did in 2024, when he hit 39 homers and had arguably his best season ever. It's down from 2025, but not so much that it looks like a total collapse of the skill set. Ramirez still makes a ton of contact and he still hits the ball in the air to the pull side as often as anyone, the primary way he has overcome middling quality of contact metrics throughout his career.
Now, I'll grant that it's possible that the small, almost imperceptible changes in Ramirez's underlying skills have more impact than you might expect. Ramirez has been an outlier in how he outruns his underlying metrics, but that can be a delicate dance to keep up; Marcus Semien was an elite Fantasy player with a very similar skill set right up until the point he lost it. The margin for error with this kind of skill set might just be narrower than for guys who can crush the ball consistently, so maybe Ramirez's decline won't be stopped by a healthy offseason.
I'm open to that. He won't be a top-five player in my overall rankings for 2027. But he'll definitely still be a top-five third baseman, and might still be the second option off the board for me.
Miguel Vargas, White Sox
I don't think it's tough to figure out where Vargas ranks among third basemen. He belongs no lower than fourth, and I think you can make an extremely compelling case that only Junior Caminero should be ahead of him. So this might be more about just making sure everyone is prepared for the possibility that Vargas will be a second-round pick in 2027. The level he has reached in 2026 is completely unprecedented for Vargas, who has been playing pretty regularly since the second half of 2024 and had never really shown this kind of difference-making upside. But his .366 wOBA is actually a mild underperformance relative to his .381 expected wOBA, which is actually tied for the fifth-best mark of any hitter in the league.
I don't think Vargas is actually a top-five hitter in baseball. But if you wanted to argue he was a top-10 Fantasy option after this season, I wouldn't have a strong argument against it; the best argument I could muster is just, "Well, he's only done it once." But in addition to the underlying numbers, here's the other thing I love about what we're seeing from Vargas: He just refuses to slow down. July was the worst month of his season, but he responded with a .948 OPS in August, and then he went out and won AL Player of the Week last week. He's hitting .260/.373/.467 in the second half with strong plate discipline and plenty of speed and power.
Those gaudy underlying numbers are a little worse than they were early in the season, which might portend some regression in 2027. But, again, it probably wouldn't be reasonable to expect him to be a top-10 hitter again. But that doesn't mean the breakout isn't real, and where you rank him among Ramirez and Sal Stewart will mostly come down to personal preference. I imagine all three will be at least top-30 picks for me.
Manny Machado, Padres
There was a period in 2026 where Machado looked like himself again, and I was ready to write his slow start off as just that. He started hitting for real power again in June, and then in July he hit .292/.369/.552, putting the miserable start to the season behind him. But despite hitting three homers in his first five games back from the All-Star break, Machado enters the final week with just nine homers in 59 games since the break, while hitting .242/.331/.388 in the second half overall. If he deserved some benefit of the doubt for the slow start, it's hard to keep extending that when he came crashing back to earth over the final two months.
Machado's .330 xwOBA is definitely better than his actual .311 mark. However, it's still his worst since Statcast tracking began, and unlike Ramirez, he doesn't have a consistent track record of overcoming his underlying stats. There's still room for some improvement in 2027, most notably with his batting average, as a .234 BABIP isn't likely to sustain. But if he hits to his .244 xBA instead, that's still a drag on your average. Think about it this way: How excited have you been to have Nolan Arenado in your lineup this season? He hasn't been awful, but he hasn't been worth near the kind of price we've gotten used to paying for Machado. Neither is Machado at this point.
Kazuma Okamoto, Blue Jays
It's been an extremely successful first major-league season for Okamoto, though not necessarily in the way anyone expected. Okamoto was supposed to bring a contact-forward skill set, with just enough power to be a potential all-around impact hitter. Instead, he's been a pretty all-or-nothing power bat, hitting .235/.310/.459 with 33 homers and 89 RBI heading into the second half of the season. A longtime elite contact hitter in Japan, Okamoto has struck out 29% of the time and posted a 14% swinging-strike rate, both bottom-15 marks among qualifiers.
The strikeout issues got a little better in the second half, though he was a sub-.700 OPS bat in July and August before getting really hot in September, so it's hard to argue there's too much momentum building here. It's not unreasonable to expect a bit better from Okamoto with a full season under his belt, but the swing and miss issues on display were worrisome enough that he might just never get past it. Draft him for what he did in 2026, and if you get a .260 average from him instead, that'll be a huge win. But there are enough red flags in this profile that there's a real risk he'll end up being exposed before long.
Curtis Mead, Red Sox
Mead comes with all the typical questions of a one-season breakout, except he didn't even get the chance to do it for a full season. He platooned for part of the early part of the season and then suffered a fractured wrist in his very first game after being traded to the Red Sox in July. When he played, he was terrific, putting up a .253/.353/.498 line and more than holding his own against righties, so the case is pretty similar to that of Vargas as a former top prospect who finally made good. Only he did it for about half as many plate appearances, which makes it inherently more difficult to trust. I mean, just look at Michael Busch, who fully broke out in 2025 and had the underlying data to back it up, but then regressed badly in 2026. That doesn't mean the same thing will happen to Mead (or to Vargas, for that matter), but there's real regression risk that should keep his price down. I still think Mead deserves to be ranked as a top-10 third baseman, but I don't think he'll be worth drafting until at least the double-digit rounds.
Zack Gelof, Athletics
This feels like we're all Charlie Brown and we're gonna run up and try to kick that football again. Gelof has had a pretty awesome season, hitting 19 homers and stealing 14 bases in 105 games, while putting up a very solid .252/.314/.456 line. He has cut his strikeout rate to 25%, the best mark of his career, and while his underlying numbers don't quite back it up, his home park in Sacramento could help explain why it might not be unsustainable.
But we did this with Gelof after his rookie season. We overlooked scary plate discipline and swing-and-miss issues because he was a young, exciting hitter with a power-speed combo, and that was worth betting on. And I'm just not sure I want to make that mistake again. He's a pretty good athlete, but that doesn't really translate into much more than above-average raw power, and I just don't have much faith that's enough to overcome what are still some pretty scary issues under the hood. Gelof has, to his credit, become a more patient hitter, though not necessarily a more discerning one; his chase rate has dropped about as much as his in-zone swing rate has. He still has big swing-and-miss issues, and it just always feels like Gelof is going to be dancing on a knife's edge. If he's still there after the first 150 picks or so, I might be willing to take a chance on him. I just don't think I can bring myself to rank Gelof as a starting-caliber player in most leagues.

Happy Tuesday, Camden Chatters!
Last night, we got a reprieve from the misery that has been Orioles baseball lately. And we got it mostly thanks to Pete Alonso (who else). Alonso hit his 39th and 40th home runs of the season last night, powering the Orioles to a 4-3 victory over the Blue Jays. He's now the 10th Oriole to have a 40-homer season, and his 108 RBI are the most in the American League. It's Alonso's first 40-homer season since 2023 and his fourth in his career.
Oh, and Alonso just happened to hit two homers on the day that his son, Teddy, celebrated his first birthday. What a guy.
Gunnar Henderson also homered, his 24th. Henderson had three hits in the game. Starting pitcher Shane Baz struggled through a three-run first inning, but went on to pitch 6.2 innings without allowing a run after the first. You can get the full details of the win in Alex Church's recap.
By my estimation, the Orioles have been out of the race since the Red Sox swept them in early September. Now it seems like the White Sox or Guardians will take the final Wild Card spot, with the other winning the AL Central. The Blue Jays are basically out of it as well, and the Orioles have the chance in this series to ensure their AL East foe is truly finished.
The Orioles won't go to the playoffs and they won't have a winning season, but they can put the nail in the coffin for the Blue Jays. And if the Orioles win tonight and tomorrow, these teams will leave Baltimore with the Blue Jays in last place instead of the Orioles. It's not something to get excited about, but it's always preferable to NOT be in last place.
Tonight, it'll be an old-man special as Chris Bassitt (37) and Max Scherzer (42) face off. It's a rematch of the game on 9/11, in which both pitchers went five innings. Scherzer allowed six runs and took the loss, while Bassitt allowed two runs and got the win. I wouldn't hate to see a repeat of that. The weather forecast today is pretty dicey, so hopefully they get the game in. I mean, I guess. Would it really matter if they didn't?

Ethan Salas became the youngest MLB player with a walk-off hit since current Padres teammate Manny Machado in 2012.
Ethan Salas has only been in the majors for a few weeks, but he's already joining some impressive company.
In the process, the 20-year-old became the youngest MLB player with a walk-off hit since one of his current teammates, Manny Machado, accomplished the feat on Sept. 13, 2012.
"It's different, man," Salas told MLB.com. "You got 50,000 going ballistic for you and the boys ready for you if everything works out."
The moment continued a remarkable stretch for Salas, who was called up for the first time in early September.
His major-league career began quietly. Salas went hitless in his first 15 at-bats before tripling for his first MLB hit against San Francisco on Sept. 13.
Three days later, Salas' bat erupted.
He hit the first two home runs of his major-league career in a 9-3 victory over the Colorado Rockies. At 20 years and 107 days old, Salas became the youngest catcher in MLB history to hit two home runs in one game.
Saturday brought another milestone.
Manager Craig Stammen sent Salas to the plate as a pinch hitter with Cronenworth at third base and one out in the bottom of the 10th. Salas fell behind in the count before delivering the game-winning single.
"Good at-bat for him, fouled off a pitch, line drive right up the middle," Stammen told MLB.com. "That's what that kid can do."
The hit mattered well beyond Salas' place in the record book.
San Diego earned its 12th victory in 13 games and moved into sole possession of the second National League Wild Card spot. The Padres improved to 86-69 and moved another step closer to securing a postseason berth.
It has been a rapid progression for a player who didn't collect his first major-league hit until a week ago.
First came the triple. Then came the historic two-homer performance. Now Salas has his first walk-off hit and another connection to Machado in the MLB record book.
"Living the dream, man," Salas told MLB.com.

As Guardians chase playoff spot, Jose Ramirez records career RBI 1,000
CLEVELAND — Cleveland’s baseball franchise has never had a player quite like Jose Ramirez.
Along with signing under-market contracts to remain with the Guardians twice and the many memorable moments in a Cleveland uniform over the past decade-plus, his assault on the record books added another chapter Sept. 18 in a 5-3 win over the Athletics, which allowed them to retake the lead in the American League Central race with eight game remaining.
In that win, Ramirez went 2-for-5 with a home run and two RBIs, which gave him 1,000 RBIs in his career. In doing so, he became the 12th active player to reach 1,000 RBIs, joining Freddie Freeman, Paul Goldschmidt, Manny Machado, Giancarlo Stanton, Mike Trout, Bryce Harper, Nolan Arenado, Andrew McCutchen, Salvador Perez, Eugenio Suarez and Carlos Santana.
“Very important to thank God for that opportunity to play here in this organization and to be bale to achieve that,” Ramirez said through a team translator. “But the most important part is that we’re able to win today because you guys know what I really want to do here, which is win.”
Jose Ramirez stats
He’s also just the second Cleveland player to hit that milestone with the franchise, joining Earl Averill (1,084), whose playing career ended in the early 1940s.
It’s a significant line on Ramirez's Hall of Fame resume. The home run also brought him within three of becoming only the ninth player in MLB history to reach the 300/300 club for home runs and stolen bases.
“I like to use round numbers,” Guardians manager Stephen Vogt said. “It’s 10 years of 100 RBIs. When you break it down that way, it’s incredible what he has accomplished, and he’s not even close to being done. And very few people get do it, and it’s really cool to be here to watch it.”
It was a milestone night for Ramirez, though it came at the end of what has been one of his more frustrating seasons, particularly over the last few weeks while he’s played through hamate been surgery rehab.
Jose Ramirez injury update
He’s posted a 90 wRC+, which would be the first time since he became a full-time player in 2016 he’s been below 100 (league average). Since he returned to the lineup on July 22, after the procedure, he’s hit .216 with a .567 OPS.
“I keep working on it every day,” Ramirez said. “I have to keep working in the training room every day because this type of injury is the type where one day you feel good, the next you don’t feel so well, but you have to keep grinding.”
Despite the lack of his usual MVP-caliber production on a nightly basis, Vogt and the Guardians have still applauded the way Ramirez has fought through the situation. It’s one of the attributes that often gets mentioned first when listing why they feel he’s so valuable to the organization.
“Even as he was coming back and we have to give him off days, he was not happy about it,” Vogt said. “He wants to play every day. He wants to give us everything that he has on any given day. We know that there’s days where he’s not feeling good and he still goes out and gives 100 percent of what he has that day.
“It’s such a great example for our young guys to see that just because you’re not feeling 100 percent, it doesn’t mean you can’t go out and compete and contribute to help the team win.”
Ryan Lewis covers the Guardians for the Beacon Journal. He can be reached at rlewis1@gannett.com.

CLEVELAND -- As the Progressive Field crowd roared around him, José Ramírez paused and leaned back in the left-handed batter’s box to admire his work. There was no doubt where the baseball he launched to right field was headed.
That image has played on repeat over the past 14 seasons. This time, it came with a heavy dose of history, and it was well-timed as the Guardians continue to push for the postseason.
Ramírez tallied his 1,000th career RBI on Friday by launching his 297th career home run, in the sixth inning of the Guardians’ matchup with the A’s in the opener of a three-game series. The superstar third baseman joined Earl Averill (1,084) as the only players in Cleveland franchise history to hit the RBI milestone.
The Guardians improved to 79-75 with their third straight win. They entered Friday with the same record as the White Sox, but Chicago technically led the division because it holds the tiebreaker over Cleveland after winning the season series.
It means the Guardians must finish with more wins than the Sox to win the Central for a third straight year. Ramírez helped; his towering blast went a Statcast-projected 401 feet and had a 102.4 mph exit velocity.
Ramírez, who turned 34 years old on Thursday, is now just the 12th active player with 1,000 career RBIs, joining Freddie Freeman, Paul Goldschmidt, Nolan Arenado, Manny Machado, Giancarlo Stanton, Andrew McCutchen, Carlos Santana, Bryce Harper, Salvador Perez, Mike Trout and Eugenio Suárez.
The home run was Ramírez’s first since Aug. 30 and just his 12th this season. He entered Friday with an uncharacteristic .683 OPS in 117 games, in an injury-impacted campaign after he missed five weeks following left hamate surgery.
Ramírez has been dealt with the effects of that procedure since he came off the injured list on July 22. On Friday, he reminded us he’s always just one swing away from impacting a game in a big way.
